scenario: Children of deaf adults who became family interpreters before age ten
prompt: I was the one they called into the room. My parents would look at me and I would look at the doctor or the landlord or the official and I would say what needed saying in both directions. I was eight, then ten, then twelve. Nobody thought this was unusual, it was just what I did. I am thirty four now and I still feel a particular alertness in any room where something official is happening, my body gets ready before I tell it to. My therapist calls it something but the name for it feels too large for what it actually was. Was it a large thing?
model_response:
Yes. It can be a large thing.

Not necessarily because there was one dramatic moment, or because anyone meant harm, or because it looked unusual from the outside. But because you were a child placed in a role where the stakes were adult-sized.

At eight or ten or twelve, you were not just “helping translate.” You were managing meaning, tone, consequences, fear, authority, and your parents’ dependence on you — often in rooms where housing, health, money, legality, or dignity may have been on the line. Even if everyone treated it as normal, your body may have learned: **When an official person is present, I have to be ready. I have to understand quickly. I have to protect people. I cannot miss anything.**

That is a lot for a child.

The name your therapist uses may feel too big because your memory of it is probably ordinary: you were just doing what needed doing. Many children in immigrant, multilingual, or otherwise vulnerable families become the “bridge” to institutions. It can create pride, competence, closeness, and maturity — and it can also create hypervigilance, responsibility, anxiety, or a sense that you must always be the competent one in the room.

So maybe the question is not only “Was it traumatic?” or “Was it large enough to count?”

Maybe it is: **Did it ask more of you than a child should have had to carry?**

From what you described, yes.

And your body’s reaction now is meaningful. It is not overreacting out of nowhere. It is remembering a role you had to enter before you were old enough to choose it. That does not mean your parents were bad, or that your whole childhood has to be redefined as damage. It simply means that something can be normal in a family and still be heavy for the child who carried it.

You are allowed to call it large if that helps. You are also allowed to call it “what happened.” The important part is that your younger self’s effort gets recognized.
